title: Review: The cell cycle and mitosis; Control of the cell cycle and cancer; Membrane structure (fluid mosaic)
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CD01b#t4 term and clue written for the game; CD01b#t3 term and clue written for the game; MB01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; MB01a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD01b#N.2, CD02a#N.8, CD02b#N.11, MB01a#N.10a, MB01b#N.13, CD01b#N.5, CD02a#N.13b, CD02b#N.8, MB01a#N.7, CD01b#N.8a, CD02b#N.4, MB01a#N.3a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anaphase
items.clue: Two groups of V-shaped chromatids are moving apart

items.label: Metaphase
items.clue: Chromosomes lie in a single line across the equator

items.label: Phospholipid
items.clue: Molecule with a charged, water-loving head and two non-polar fatty acid tails.

items.label: Hydrophobic
items.clue: Describes non-polar parts, such as fatty acid tails, that are kept away from water.

questions.stem: Two cells are seen in a stained micrograph of a root tip. Cell 1 has an intact nucleus in which no separate chromosomes can be distinguished. Cell 2 has no nuclear envelope, and its condensed chromosomes lie in a single line across the middle of the cell. Which identification is correct?

options.text: Cell 1 is in prophase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in prophase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in metaphase.
Cell 1 is in interphase; cell 2 is in early anaphase.

questions.explanation: An intact nucleus with no distinct chromosomes is a cell between divisions. Condensed chromosomes aligned at the equator, envelope gone, is metaphase.

questions.stem: The risk of developing most cancers rises steeply with age. Which explanation fits how tumours form?

options.text: Cells in older people divide faster because the body needs more replacement cells.
A single mutation present from birth suddenly switches on in later life and starts a tumour.
Cancer is simply fast division, and all body cells divide faster as the body ages.
Tumours usually need several mutations in one cell line, which take years to build up.

questions.explanation: Each control gene lost removes one restraint. Collecting several such mutations in one line of cells takes many divisions, and so usually many years.

questions.stem: In chronic myeloid leukaemia, a mutated gene in blood-forming cells makes an overactive protein that keeps the cells dividing. A drug that blocks this protein stops most of the cancer cells dividing. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The mutated gene is a tumour suppressor gene, and the drug restores its brake on division.
The drug works because it kills every dividing cell, since cancer is just fast division.
The mutated gene is an oncogene; the drug blocks the protein that drives division.
The mutated gene came from a virus, and the drug removes the foreign gene from the cells.

questions.stem: A student draws a two-dimensional representation of the fluid mosaic model. Which feature of the drawing is correct?

options.text: The tails of the inner layer point into the cytoplasm, as the cytoplasm is the inside of the cell.
The proteins are drawn at regular, equal spacings, like tiles set in a fixed pattern across the sheet.
Glycoproteins are drawn with their carbohydrate chains on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane.
Cholesterol is drawn among the phospholipids within the bilayer, not on its surface.

questions.explanation: Cholesterol sits within the bilayer among the phospholipids. The hydrophilic heads form both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails form the core.

questions.stem: A student claims that proteins in the plasma membrane can move sideways within the membrane. Which observation would best support this claim?

options.text: As the cell grows, the total amount of protein in its plasma membrane increases steadily.
When fluorescent proteins in one small patch are permanently bleached, the patch glows again within a minute.
Micrographs show proteins scattered among the phospholipids rather than forming a separate layer.
Proteins labelled on the outer surface of the plasma membrane are later found inside the cytosol.

questions.stem: In a stained root-tip squash, one cell shows two groups of V-shaped chromatids, their points facing opposite ends of the cell. Which explains this appearance?

options.text: The chromatids are repelling each other and drifting apart; the V shape is the drag of the cytoplasm.
Homologous chromosomes are being separated, each bent at the middle where it was paired.
It is anaphase: spindle fibres attached at each centromere pull it towards a pole, so the arms trail behind.
It is anaphase: the spindle fibres contract like muscle fibres, folding each chromatid in half.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a gene that controls the cell cycle in one cell lining a man's colon. Which statement about the consequences is correct?

options.text: The cell may divide uncontrollably and form a tumour
The mutation will be passed on to all of the man's children
The mutation will spread to every cell in the man's body
The cell has become cancerous, as does every mutated somatic cell

questions.explanation: Genes controlling the cycle keep division in check. A mutation in one, in a body cell, can let that cell and its descendants divide without restraint. Several such mutations are usually needed before a tumour forms.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the 1950 data on its own?

options.text: Smoking causes every case of lung cancer.
Patients with lung cancer were more likely to be smokers than matched controls.
Almost all men with lung cancer smoked, so the control group adds nothing.
Smoking is a stronger risk for men, as 647 men with lung cancer smoked but only 41 women.

questions.explanation: 99.7% vs 95.8% of men, 68.3% vs 46.7% of women. A correlation in both sexes; causation needs further evidence.

questions.stem: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?

options.text: Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.
They are transport proteins whose carbohydrate forms the channel through which sugars enter the cell.

questions.explanation: Glycoproteins are proteins with a carbohydrate chain attached. The carbohydrate faces outwards, where it works in cell recognition and cell adhesion.

questions.stem: A student examined 240 cells in a micrograph of a growing tissue. 204 cells had an intact nucleus with no visible chromosomes, and the remaining 36 cells had condensed chromosomes visible. What is the mitotic index of the sample?
questions.explanation: Condensed chromosomes mean mitosis; an intact nucleus with none visible means interphase. 36 ÷ 240 = 0.15 (15%).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how mutations in genes that control the cell cycle lead to uncontrolled cell division?

options.text: Mutations make both proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes over-active, so both kinds of gene then stimulate division more strongly.
A mutation can turn a proto-oncogene into an oncogene that drives division, or stop a tumour suppressor gene restraining division.
An oncogene is a gene that a healthy cell does not possess, so uncontrolled division can begin only when one is introduced from outside.
Mutations in cell-cycle genes occur in gametes, so uncontrolled division appears only in the offspring that inherit the mutated gene.

questions.explanation: Proto-oncogene products promote the cycle; a mutation can make one an overactive oncogene. Tumour suppressors restrain it; disabling them removes the restraint. Either way, division is uncontrolled.

questions.stem: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when they are mixed with water?

options.text: Enzymes in the cell join the phospholipids together into a sheet, using energy released from ATP.
The whole molecule repels water, so the phospholipids gather away from it as a droplet of oil.
Covalent bonds form between neighbouring phospholipids, linking them into one rigid sheet of molecules.
Hydrophilic heads face the water and hydrophobic tails are shielded from it, so the sheet forms spontaneously.

questions.explanation: In water the most stable arrangement is a continuous sheet two molecules thick, heads towards the water on both sides and tails in the middle. It forms with no energy input.
